name: The Birthday Problem
statement: In a group of just 23 people, two probably share a birthday.
statementAccent: just 23 people, two probably share a birthday
meaning: The birthday paradox is the surprising fact that in a group of only 23 people the probability that at least two share a birthday is already greater than one half, about 50.7 percent, and by 70 people it is around 99.9 percent. It is called a paradox not because it is self-contradictory but because it clashes so sharply with intuition: most people guess you would need something closer to half of 365. The result is a staple lesson in how badly human intuition handles combinations and probabilities, and it has a serious edge in cryptography, where the same counting underlies attacks on hash functions.
mechanism: The key is that the comparison is over pairs, not people. With 23 people there are 23 times 22 divided by 2, or 253 distinct pairs, and each pair is a separate chance for a match. The probability is easiest to compute by its complement: work out the chance that all 23 birthdays are different, by multiplying 365 over 365, times 364 over 365, and so on down, which comes to about 0.4927, and subtract from one to get roughly 0.5073. The confusion arises because people instinctively solve a different problem, whether anyone shares their own particular birthday, which really would need about 253 other people to reach even odds.

examples.text: Twenty-three people give roughly a 50.7 percent chance of a shared birthday, the headline figure that reliably astonishes audiences.
By 70 people the chance passes 99.9 percent, and by 367 a shared birthday is guaranteed outright by the pigeonhole principle, since there are only 366 possible dates.

The same square-root mathematics makes finding a hash collision far cheaper than brute force, only about the square root of the number of possible outputs, which is why cryptographic hashes must be long.

variants.name: The pigeonhole principle
variants.text: The deterministic backstop: with only 366 possible birthdays, 367 people force a shared one with certainty (a guarantee, where the birthday problem is about likelihood at just 23).

variants.name: The birthday attack
variants.text: The cryptographic application: collisions among values drawn from a large space become likely near the square root of its size, setting the required length of hash functions.

whyItMatters: The birthday paradox is one of the clearest demonstrations that human intuition systematically underestimates the likelihood of coincidences, because we think in terms of individuals rather than the far more numerous pairs. Beyond its value as a teaching example in probability, it has concrete consequences in computer science and cryptography, where the birthday bound sets the security margin of hash functions and dictates that collision resistance requires roughly twice the output length of preimage resistance. It is a small puzzle with a long reach into how we reason about chance and how we secure information.

working.text: gauge coincidence likelihood by the number of pairs, which grows with the square of the group size, not by the head count.

working.lead: Use the square-root rule of thumb
working.text: expect collisions to become likely once a sample nears the square root of the number of possible categories.

working.lead: Size hashes against the birthday bound
working.text: in cryptography, choose hash lengths so that the square-root collision cost stays infeasible.

limits: The classic figures assume all 365 days are equally likely, that birthdays are independent, and that leap-day births are ignored. Real birthdays are not perfectly uniform, but any unevenness only makes shared birthdays slightly more likely, never less, so 23 is if anything a conservative threshold. The result is exact within these idealisations and shifts only marginally in the real world. The paradox is a statement about the probability of some shared birthday among any pair, and its figures do not transfer to the different question of matching one particular, fixed birthday.
misreadings: It does not say 23 people are enough for someone to share your birthday; that far rarer event needs about 253 people, and confusing the two is the heart of the illusion. It does not require anywhere near 183 people, half of 365, which is the wrong intuition it corrects. And non-uniform real-world birthdays do not weaken the effect but slightly strengthen it, so the everyday world makes coincidences a touch more common, not less.
origin: A classic result of elementary probability with no single clean originator: the problem is generally attributed to Harold Davenport around 1927, though he did not publish it, and the first published version was by Richard von Mises in 1939.
